paper_title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

sections.title: Model
sections.content: 1. Introduction The rapid advancement of reasoning, code generation, and tool interaction in large language models (LLMs) is enabling artificial intelligence (AI) to move beyond assisting scientific research and engineering toward autonomously developing and improving AI systems. These efforts include model training, optimization of solver programs, and algorithm design, making AI for AI (AI4AI) research direction toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In this context, machine learning engineering (MLE) provides concrete setting for this goal, requiring long-horizon optimization through repeated execution, feedback analysis, and revision rather than one-shot generation. Most existing MLE systems [1, 2, 3] extend code generation into iterative optimization through search, memory, or multi-agent collaboration. As shown in Figure 1(a), predefined workflows or search rules typically control experiment sequencing and stage transitions, while LLMs primarily generate or debug code at designated steps. These systems rely heavily on manually designed control logic to : Corresponding Authors : Co-first Authors Please send correspondence regarding this report to yanxiangchao@pjlab.org.cn and zhangbo@pjlab.org.cn. : Project Lead Figure 1 Decision making in long-horizon MLE optimization. (a) External orchestration organizes optimization through predefined workflows and search rules. (b) In model-directed interaction, the model selects subsequent actions based on experimental states and execution feedback. organize long-horizon experimentation. Recently, Arbor [4] and Argus [5] maintain persistent research states and allow models to design, continue, and revise experiments, placing greater demands on the models ability to plan experiments and sustain optimization over long interaction horizons. ML-Agent [6] combines multi-turn demonstrations with single-step RL, while Frontis-MA1 [7] trains program evolution operators through SFT and RL and integrates them into an external evolutionary search framework. These approaches primarily train models for single-step decisions or local operations within externally organized processes. In contrast, we study how to train models to organize experiments and improve solutions over sustained interaction, using experience and execution feedback from real-world MLE tasks. However, training this long-horizon optimization capability poses three challenges. 1) Open-ended MLE requires an interaction environment that preserves experimental states while leaving action selection to the model. 2) High-quality long-horizon supervision is difficult to obtain because MLE tasks are heterogeneous and interaction trajectories may mix useful exploration and failure recovery with degraded decisions. 3) Each costly experiment returns feedback on several preceding decisions before the full run ends; online RL must use this intermediate signal while handling policy mismatch during asynchronous collection. To address these challenges, we propose post-training method for autonomous MLE that combines model-directed long-horizon interaction harness, hierarchical agentic SFT, and Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning (WIRL). Based on this, we train MLExpert, 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model, to learn long-horizon optimization strategies. As shown in Figure 1(b), MLExpert uses sustained tool interaction within the interaction harness to autonomously organize experiments, revise solutions based on execution feedback, and maintain submission candidates. We build the Kaggle-MLE Factory to convert historical Kaggle competitions into executable MLE tasks. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE optimization, with execution outcomes guiding the selection of trajectories and segments for supervision. To use this intermediate feedback, WIRL treats each completed experiment as the boundary of an execution window containing decisions since the previous result. It trains those decisions with shared outcome-based reward, while asynchronous collection and policy correction allow updates as trajectories continue. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. MLExpert also improves performance on NatureBench Lite and transfers its optimization capabilities to agent scaffold and algorithm optimization tasks. Our key contributions are: We introduce MLExpert, 35B MoE model for autonomous MLE, trained with hierarchical agentic 2 SFT and WIRL. WIRL links execution feedback to multi-turn decisions within execution windows and combines local progress rewards with policy correction for asynchronous online learning. We build the Kaggle-MLE Factory and an Interaction Harness to provide executable tasks and model-directed long-horizon interaction for training and evaluation. Extensive experiments show that MLExpert improves the base models average medal rate from 37.9% to 72.7% on MLE-Bench Lite, improves performance on NatureBench Lite, and generalizes to agent scaffold and algorithm optimization tasks. 2. Preliminary We formulate MLE as the iterative optimization of executable ML solutions within given time budget 𝐵𝑒. An MLE task is represented as 𝑒 = (𝑑𝑒, D𝑒, 𝑚𝑒), where 𝑑𝑒 is the task description, D𝑒 is the task data, and 𝑚𝑒 is the evaluation metric. candidate solution 𝑦 Y𝑒 represents complete ML pipeline including data processing, feature engineering, model training, and prediction, where Y𝑒 denotes the solution space. The objective is to find best-performing solution for given task, 𝑦 𝑆𝑒( 𝑦), where 𝑆𝑒( 𝑦) denotes the task-specific score under metric 𝑚𝑒, normalized so 𝑒 arg max𝑦 Y𝑒 that higher values indicate better performance. Following MLE-bench [8], the agent has access to the task description and public data, and improves solutions through code execution and self-constructed validation. The final submission is independently evaluated using hidden test labels. In Agentic MLE, an LLM policy 𝜋𝜃 autonomously organizes the optimization process. Given task 𝑒, the model constructs, executes, and improves candidate solutions through continuous tool interaction within the time budget 𝐵𝑒. trajectory of length 𝐿 is represented as 𝜏 = (𝑜0, 𝑎0, 𝑜1, 𝑎1, . . . , 𝑎𝐿1, 𝑜𝐿), where 𝑜0 is the initial task observation, 𝑎𝑙 is the model action at step 𝑙, and 𝑜𝑙+1 is the observation returned after executing 𝑎𝑙. Each action may include model reasoning and one or more tool calls. At step 𝑙, the model samples 𝑎𝑙 𝜋𝜃( 𝑐𝑙), where 𝑐𝑙 consists of the task information and retained interaction history. Experimental states, including code, execution records, and candidate solutions, are stored in an external workspace and exposed to the model through tool observations. Rather than following predefined workflow, the model decides when to analyze, revise, execute, or change the optimization direction based on the current state. The model maintains submission candidate throughout the interaction and selects its final solution ˆ𝑦𝜏 at the end of trajectory 𝜏 based on the experimental results and analysis available during interaction. Task Construction and Long-Horizon Interaction As shown in Figure 2, we build the Kaggle-MLE Factory to provide executable tasks and the Interaction Harness to support model-directed long-horizon experimentation and state management, together enabling hierarchical agentic SFT and WIRL for post-training MLExpert in autonomous MLE. 3.1. Kaggle-MLE Factory: Constructing Executable MLE Tasks Long-horizon Agentic MLE training requires executable tasks covering diverse data modalities, objectives, and domains. Historical Kaggle competitions provide rich source of real-world MLE problems, 3 Figure 2 Overview of MLExpert training for autonomous MLE. The Kaggle-MLE Factory constructs executable tasks, and the interaction harness supports model-directed experimentation and trajectory collection. Hierarchical agentic SFT learns from demonstrations, while WIRL further optimizes the policy from execution feedback collected during online interaction. but their heterogeneous data organization, submission formats, and evaluation protocols make manual task adaptation difficult to scale. Therefore, we build the Kaggle-MLE Factory, which converts historical competitions into executable tasks with public workspace, hidden test split, and unified evaluation interface. The Factory uses multi-agent pipeline for task construction, validation, and repair. The discovery agent filters competitions by status, scale, and submission format. After competition data, leaderboard information, and official descriptions are collected, the analyzer agent extracts data structures, fields, and modality characteristics to form task specification. The generator agent then prepares task data, constructs held-out test split with hidden labels from the original labeled data, and implements the task-specific evaluator. The task is executed on real data and iteratively repaired based on validator checks of data integrity, submission format, and evaluation behavior to produce valid executable tasks. Standardized task packages support different MLE agent frameworks. Final manual review excludes tasks with unresolved label or scoring issues before trajectory collection. Appendix details agent responsibilities and implementation. 3.2. Interaction Harness for Long-Horizon MLE Optimization To support model-directed long-horizon MLE optimization, we design an interaction harness that follows ReAct-style loop [9], leaving branch selection and optimization-path decisions to the model rather than an external search policy. The harness stores experimental states in solution nodes, each containing candidate code, execution logs, and metadata. Parent-linked revisions form an experiment tree that the model can revisit and compare to decide whether to continue, backtrack, or change optimization direction. The harness provides tools for solution analysis, code revision, experiment execution, history retrieval, and submission management. The model launches candidate execution through execute_code and updates its submission candidate through update_answer. The complete tool list and descriptions are provided in Appendix B. As interaction history approaches the context limit, earlier messages are summarized while recent interactions are retained. For complex analysis, analyze delegates task analysis, data exploration, and result diagnosis to an analysis sub-agent with independent context, returning only summary to the main model. Since overfitting or data leakage can inflate validation scores, the model can call 4 invalidate_node based on experimental evidence and analysis to exclude unreliable candidates. With new evidence, the model can update its submission candidate while exploring alternatives. 4. Agentic MLE Post-Training 4.1. Hierarchical Agentic SFT Long-horizon MLE optimization requires general tool-use, coding skills, and domain-specific decision making. We therefore use two-stage hierarchical agentic SFT. In the first stage, coding and tool-use trajectories from diverse agentic tasks are used to learn basic tool-use and code revision capabilities. The second stage adopts teacher trajectories from MLE domain and literature-derived scientific tasks to improve algorithm design, experimental analysis, and iterative optimization. Complementary MLE demonstrations. MLE adaptation data cover both task initialization and sustained optimization. For trajectories whose first complete solution executes successfully and reaches quality threshold, we extract the interaction prefix from task start through the corresponding execution feedback as an initial-solution trajectory, typically covering task understanding, algorithm design, and code generation. We also use long-horizon optimization trajectories from complete interactions, covering solution construction, feedback analysis, iterative revision, and final submission selection. In addition, analysis sub-agent trajectories are adopted to train the model for independent data analysis and result diagnosis. Outcome-guided supervision selection. Long-horizon MLE trajectories can contain effective exploration and failure recovery, but may also include misguided decisions or continued degradation after reaching strong solution. Therefore, we use execution results of submitted solutions to select high-quality trajectories and the segments used for supervision. For trajectories that pass quality threshold, we identify the first best-performing submission and measure the subsequent performance degradation. When the post-peak degradation exceeds threshold, we use the first best-performing submission as the anchor for retaining trajectory prefix; otherwise, we use the last submission. The prefix ends at complete tool-interaction boundary near the anchor. This removes degraded tails while preserving useful exploration and failure recovery before the peak. Supervision samples and training objective. To preserve multi-turn context dependencies, each supervision sample combines existing interaction context with continuous sequence of subsequent model actions and environment feedback from the selected MLE interactions. When context compaction occurs, the retained history and summary form the conditioning context for subsequent samples. Training loss is applied only to newly generated reasoning, text responses, and tool-call tokens, while tool feedback and inherited interaction history are used only as conditioning context and masked out from the loss. Details of outcome-guided filtering, score normalization, and the SFT objective appear in Appendix C.1. 4.2. Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning Building on SFT, we further optimize the long-horizon decision policy using execution feedback from the models own exploration. In MLE, solution quality is available only after training and evaluation, and each result depends on multiple rounds of analysis, code revision, and tool interaction. We introduce Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL), which groups consecutive model decisions made between successive experiment results into an execution window 𝑢𝑚. Each window is conditioned on the accumulated interaction history and associated with the outcome of the corresponding experiment launched through the execute_code tool (Sec. 3.2). The first window starts from the initial task state. This allows policy updates to use feedback from completed experiments without waiting for the entire task trajectory to finish. Window rewards and shared optimization weights. MLE tasks use different evaluation metrics and score scales, so we use task-specific medal thresholds as common reference for solution quality and compare each valid submission with the most recent valid submission in the trajectory to capture local optimization progress. The reward of execution window 𝑢𝑚 is 𝑅𝑚 = 1.0, 0.6, 0.4 + 𝑇𝑚, 1.0 + 𝑇𝑚, 2.0 + 𝑇𝑚, execution error caused by model actions, no such error but no scorable submission, valid submission below the medal threshold, bronze or silver medal, gold medal. (2) Here, 𝑇𝑚 denotes the local performance trend and is set to 0 for the first valid submission. For subsequent valid submissions, 𝑇𝑚 {0.2, 0, 0.2} according to whether performance decreases, remains unchanged, or improves relative to the previous valid submission, accounting for the direction of the task metric. All five metrics are computed over the 22 tasks and reported as percentages. We also evaluate on NatureBench [12], following the ten-task Lite subset used in Frontis-MA1 [7]. Baselines. We compare MLExpert against two groups of models: (1) same-scale models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [13], Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B [14], and Nex-N2.5-mini [15]; and (2) larger frontier models, including DeepSeek-V4-Pro Preview [16], MiniMax M3 [17], GLM-5.3 [18], Kimi-K3 [19], GPT-5.5 [20], and GPT-5.6 Sol [21]. Implementation details. Each MLE task is assigned maximum of 3,000 interaction steps and 12hour runtime, using 20 vCPUs, 220 GB of RAM, and single NVIDIA H200 GPU. MLExpert is initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. General SFT uses coding and tool-use trajectories from StepFun [22]. For MLE SFT, we collect teacher trajectories from Kaggle-MLE Factory tasks, MLE-Dojo [23] tasks, and scientific tasks derived from Nature-family papers. Any training tasks overlapping with MLE-Bench or NatureBench [12] are excluded. Data statistics, training hyperparameters, and implementation details are provided in Appendix C. 5.2. Main Results MLExpert achieves the highest medal rate among same-scale models and reaches the performance level of larger frontier models. As shown in Table 1, under the unified MLExpert Harness, MLExpert raises the medal rate of its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving the highest rate among the same-scale models evaluated and performance comparable to GLM-5.3 and Kimi-K3. MLExpert retains its advantage over the base model under general-purpose coding harness. With Claude Code, MLExpert achieves 69.7% medal rate, compared with 42.4% for its base model, and exceeds the strongest evaluated same-scale baseline by 22.7 percentage points. The consistent advantage over the base model across both harnesses suggests that the improvement from posttraining is not specific to the MLExpert-Harness and remains effective in general-purpose agentic coding environment. On NatureBench Lite, MLExpert improves scientific task performance over the base model. Table 2 shows that, with Claude Code, MLExpert raises the Surpass-SOTA rate from 0.0% to 50.0%, exceeding Nex-N2.5-mini at 20.0% and matching GLM-5.3 at 50.0%. Its Match-SOTA rate also improves from 40.0% to 70.0%. These results show that post-training improves scientific task optimization, enabling MLExpert to match or exceed published reference results on more tasks. 5.3. Effect of post-training stages. Table 3 compares successive training stages under the MLExpert Harness. General Agent SFT raises the average medal rate from 37.9% to 47.0%, MLE-domain SFT 8 further increases it to 62.1%, and WIRL reaches 72.7%. Each stage provides an additional gain. In particular, hierarchical SFT substantially improves MLE performance over the base model, while WIRL further improves performance beyond teacher-supervised training through online execution feedback. RL baselines and key WIRL design choices. We compare WIRL with trajectory-level GRPO and PPOstyle optimization under the same MLE environment and MLE-SFT initialization. GRPO uses grouprelative advantages, whereas PPO-style optimization uses clipped objective weighted by terminal trajectory rewards without an additional critic. We also evaluate WIRL variants that remove the trend reward or policy correction separately. As shown in Table 4, GRPO and PPO-style optimization achieve 56.1% and 60.6%, respectively, both below the 62.1% achieved by MLE-SFT, supporting WIRLs overall design of learning from execution-window feedback. In contrast, the two WIRL variants reach 66.7% and 65.2%, respectively, while full WIRL further improves the medal rate to 72.7%, indicating that both the local trend reward and policy correction contribute to the final improvement. Further analysis in Appendix D.1 shows that asynchronous execution-window collection reduces the learner waiting fraction compared with trajectory-based GRPO. 5.4. Case Study: Long-Horizon Optimization Figure 3 Long-horizon optimization on MLSP 2013 Birds. (a) Representative optimization progress of MLExpert. (b) Initial and final ROC-AUC for Base, MLExpert-SFT, and MLExpert. To examine the long-horizon optimization behavior of MLExpert, we select MLSP 2013 Birds as representative case. Figure 3(a) traces the optimization process from audio features and LightGBM through PANNs representations to AST fine-tuning with attention pooling and an MLP head, followed by training-schedule adjustments and snapshot averaging. As shown in Figure 3(b), MLExpert and MLExpert-SFT start with solutions of similar quality, but MLExpert improves ROC-AUC from 0.58 to 0.964, compared with 0.60 to 0.88 for MLExpert-SFT. This case shows how MLExpert continues to improve solutions through sustained experimentation and execution feedback. 5.5. Generalization to Other Optimization Tasks Agent scaffold optimization. Following ShinkaEvolve [24], we optimize Python scaffold for fixed GPT-4.1-nano solver on AIME 2025 [25] and evaluate it on AIME problems from years not used for optimization. Table 5 shows that the scaffold optimized by MLExpert achieves 43.7% held-out accuracy, compared with 23.3% for the scaffold optimized by the base model. These results show that post-training improves the ability to design effective agent workflows, with optimization gains extending to unseen problems. Full protocols and task-level results are provided in Appendix D.4. Figure 4 Algorithm-component optimization on 12 selected MLS-Bench-Lite tasks. Bars show normalized verifier rewards for Base and MLExpert. 6. Related work 6.1. Agents for Automated ML Research LLM agents increasingly automate data analysis, model development, and experimental iteration, with recent work extending to autonomous AI system design and improvement [27]. AIDE [1] and MLESTAR [2] improve candidate solutions through iterative search and refinement, while MLEvolve [28] and MARS [29] use structured treeor graph-based search, memory, and planning to organize longhorizon experimentation. R&D-Agent [3] studies multi-role collaboration, while InternAgent [30] and FM-Agent [31] extend autonomous AI research across machine learning, algorithm optimization, and engineering tasks. Recent systems including Arbor [4] and Argus [5] maintain persistent research states and increase model control. 10 Recent work develops MLE capabilities by training models on interaction experience. ML-Agent [6] combines multi-turn demonstrations with single-step RL, while RL for MLE Agents [32], MLE-RL [33], and AceGRPO [34] study online MLE training with execution feedback, asynchronous sampling, or intermediate trajectory states. Learning to Ideate [35] trains models to generate algorithm improvement suggestions, whereas Frontis-MA1 [7] applies SFT and RL to program evolution operators and combines them through an external evolutionary framework. These approaches primarily train individual interaction steps or local components of externally organized optimization workflows. SandMLE [36] applies trajectory-wise on-policy RL in micro-scale synthetic MLE environments. We train model-directed long-horizon interaction policies on real-world MLE tasks, with WIRL using execution windows to learn multi-turn decisions from delayed execution feedback under asynchronous updates. 6.2. Post-Training Long-Horizon Agentic Models Recent research has increasingly focused on post-training agentic models for sustained interaction, complex tool use, and long-horizon decision making. SWE-Gym [37] trains coding agents using trajectories collected from executable environments, while Search-R1 [38] and WebRL [39] learn multi-turn tool use from environment feedback and outcome rewards. AgentFlow [40] directly optimizes planning policies in general multi-turn agentic interaction and uses trajectory-level outcomes to train intermediate decisions. Recent work has also explored generalist agentic models for longhorizon interaction. Agents-A1 [41] uses long-horizon knowledge-action trajectories and multi-stage training, together with multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD), to combine capabilities from multiple domain teachers into unified model. Ornith-1.5 [14] extends self-scaffolding by jointly optimizing task generation, scaffold construction, and solution rollouts through RL. 7. Conclusion In this work, we introduce MLExpert, 35B MoE agentic model trained to autonomously conduct and improve machine learning experiments over long interaction horizons. We build an automated MLE task factory and model-directed interaction harness, and train MLExpert with hierarchical agentic SFT and WIRL to learn from teacher demonstrations and execution feedback collected from its own exploration. Extensive experiments show that MLExpert improves over its base model on MLE-Bench Lite and achieves performance comparable to larger frontier models. Further improvements on NatureBench Lite and in agent scaffold and algorithm optimization demonstrate cross-task generalization. These results support treating long-horizon optimization decision making as trainable model capability, providing practical path toward autonomous machine learning engineering and scientific experimentation.

Details of the Kaggle-MLE Factory We begin with Meta-Kaggle1 competition metadata snapshot containing 11,649 entries. Guided by the task-selection principles of MLE-bench [8], the discovery agent considers task relevance, data availability, and the feasibility of offline evaluation. Automated initial screening uses competition completion, at least 50 participating teams, and dataset size limit of 200 GB as default criteria, checks submission-interface compatibility, and consults an exclusion list of existing tasks. The agent further selects candidates across domains and data modalities, including vision, text, audio, tabular data, and time series. Candidates are collected and processed in multiple batches. The downloader and scraper retrieve competition data, official descriptions, and leaderboard information. The analyzer agent extracts data structures, field information, and modality characteristics to form task specification, which the generator agent uses to produce data-preparation and scoring code. When test labels are unavailable, the pipeline constructs held-out split from the original labeled data and keeps its labels on the evaluation side. The executor runs generated task packages on real data, while the validator agent checks structural completeness, submission-format consistency, non-degenerate labels, traintest identifier overlap, and data availability. The validator also executes the scoring function to check that it produces valid score. Execution and validation errors are returned to the construction agents for repair. We conduct final human review of the 160 registered tasks, excluding six with unresolved label or scoring-implementation issues and retaining 154 tasks for subsequent trajectory collection. B. Interaction Harness Tools The Interaction Harness described in Section 3.2 provides tools for inspecting the task environment, revising candidate solutions, running experiments, retrieving previous states, and managing submissions. Figure 5 compares the learner waiting fractions of GRPO and WIRL under the same training setup. The waiting fraction is the time spent waiting for training data divided by the sum of waiting and training time. Over the recorded updates, the mean per-update waiting fraction is 87.6% for GRPO and 39.3% for WIRL, difference of 48.3 percentage points. WIRL exhibits substantially lower learner waiting overhead during RL training. D.2. NatureBench Lite We use the ten-task NatureBench Lite subset listed by Frontis-MA1 [7], with the and definitions from NatureBench [12]. We follow the official NatureBench evaluation protocol, with four-hour runtime budget per task that excludes time spent scoring submissions. Following NatureBench, we compute the normalized relative gap for each evaluation instance by subtracting the paper-reported SOTA value from the agents primary metric value, adjusting the sign so that improvements are positive, and dividing by the absolute SOTA value. Instances without valid submission receive gap of 1. The task-level score 𝑔 is the mean gap across instances. Match-SOTA and Surpass-SOTA report the percentages of tasks with 𝑔 0 and 𝑔 > 0.1, respectively. We report single evaluation of MLExpert over the ten tasks, with Surpass-SOTA on five tasks and Match-SOTA on seven tasks, corresponding to 50.0% and 70.0%, respectively. DeepSeek-V4-Pro Preview and MiniMax M3 [17] 20 results are taken from Table 2 of Frontis-MA1. Our NatureBench evaluations use NVIDIA H200 GPUs; external reference results retain their original evaluation conditions. Matching and surpassing scientific reference results. Under Claude Code, MLExpert improves Surpass-SOTA from 0.0% to 50.0% and Match-SOTA from 40.0% to 70.0% relative to the base model. Compared with Nex-N2.5-mini, MLExpert has higher Surpass-SOTA rate, 50.0% versus 20.0%, but lower Match-SOTA rate, 70.0% versus 80.0%. MLExpert more frequently exceeds the reference by the Surpass-SOTA margin, while Nex matches the reference on larger fraction of evaluations. MLExpert matches the 50.0% Surpass-SOTA rate of GLM-5.3, whose Match-SOTA rate is higher at 90.0%. D.3. AIME Agent Scaffold Optimization The outer model optimizes Python agent scaffold that calls fixed gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14 solver. All optimizers start from the same single-query scaffold and share the task environment, tools, and evaluator. Each search has four-hour time limit and maximum of 1,000 interaction steps, with context limit of 200,000 tokens and an output limit of 65,536 tokens per step. The scaffold can modify prompting, calling, verification, voting, and answer-extraction procedures, with at most ten inner-model calls per problem. Initial uses one solver call, while Majority@5 takes majority vote over five independently sampled answers. Development uses all 30 problems from AIME 2025, with three evaluations per problem for each candidate scaffold. The outer model receives aggregate accuracy, call counts, and sanitized error summaries. Exact-request response caching is used during development to reuse inner-solver responses to identical requests. After search, the selected scaffold is frozen and evaluated using fresh solver calls on AIME 2023, 2024, and 2026. Each held-out year contains 30 problems and is evaluated three times; these years provide no feedback for scaffold development or selection. Thus, each optimizer contributes one frozen scaffold, with three evaluation repetitions per year. Accuracy is the fraction of answers that exactly match the reference integer answer; missing or incorrectly formatted answers count as incorrect. Table 11 reports development accuracy, accuracy for each held-out year, the mean across the three held-out years, and mean inner-model calls per problem on the held-out evaluations. Each annual accuracy averages the three evaluations of that years 30 problems. Solver-call efficiency after SFT. The scaffold optimized by MLExpert-SFT achieves 38.1% heldout accuracy with 3.51 solver calls per problem, approaching the 40.0% achieved by Kimi-K3 with approximately 59% fewer calls. It also outperforms Majority@5, which reaches 24.8% with five calls per problem. MLExpert-SFT therefore improves held-out accuracy over fixed majority voting while using fewer solver calls, suggesting that its optimized scaffold uses the solver more effectively. These results indicate that SFT already supports effective scaffold optimization across held-out years. Further gains from WIRL. WIRL raises held-out accuracy from 38.1% to 43.7%, gain of 5.6 percentage points, with improvements on all three held-out years. The resulting scaffold uses 8.40 calls per problem, compared with 3.51 for MLExpert-SFT and 8.65 for Kimi-K3. With similar number of calls to Kimi-K3, MLExpert exceeds its 40.0% accuracy, while GLM-5.3 achieves 48.1% with 9.39 calls. The SFT and RL results therefore offer different accuracycall trade-offs: SFT yields an effective scaffold with fewer calls, while further RL finds more accurate scaffold that uses more calls. D.4.
